title: Club dates, weddings and bar mitzvahs
summary: He talks about doing several club dates a weekend, playing disco and horas, and why such gigs are valuable training.

blocks.x: That’s really interesting. I had heard other terms but not that one in particular. I mean we did it when I was — in the rock & roll days we did similar stuff, but that’s really great. And I chuckled today because, I forget what the question was at the concert, and you mentioned a tune, you were talking about playing gigs to put food on the table.
And you mentioned the tune “Cherry Pink and Apple Blossom White” and I played that song last night.
Sure. That’s funny. You do what’s required.

Well you know I think that colleges, as part of jazz education should teach these young musicians how to play a gig like that. I think that would be really valuable. Because you get out of school and I mean I used to do four or five — you know we’d call them club dates. Some people call them casuals. I think it depends on what part of the country you come from. But it’s a wedding or a bar mitzvah basically. And you know sometimes I would do five of those on a weekend. You know, two on Friday, two on Saturday — no one on Friday, two on Saturday and two on Sunday. And that’s hard. Because they’re four hour gigs and if you play a cocktail hour that’s a five hour gig. So that, and plus you have to drive. You have to drive from one gig to the other, set up, play, and you know most of the music is pretty horrendous. I mean this is when disco was around, so we’d play a lot of disco tunes. But I was doing — I mean I was playing with Kenny Warner, Billy Drews, I mean we used to have like a horn section with five horns. And a full rhythm section and a bunch of singers. And we would have these big full-blown productions. That would cost a lot of money for the families. But at least we were all together playing music with our friends. And it’s not so easy, just from a mental standpoint, to have to play Hava Nagila five times on a weekend, and that’s just one hora. We used to play medlies of horas. You know, play a half hour hora medley. But you have to know the tunes.

H-O-R-A. No not whore. No hora. It’s a particular form of Jewish dance, that you play at Jewish weddings or bar mitzvahs. Anyway, so we used to play tons of these things. So do you want to at least have the instrument in your mouth when you’re playing? Or do you © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -12-

want to work at a diner flipping burgers or being a waiter? You know I think it would be a good idea to teach, I mean granted I haven’t done a club date in many, many, many years, so I don’t know if people still do them or if now there’s DJ’s. So I don’t even know if people have live music at a dance anymore. The way the music business is going, Broadway and shows, it could be, who knows? It could be that whole scene where having a live band at a wedding or a bar mitzvah could be finished. I really don’t know, I’m not involved in that world anymore.
Yeah. The DJ’s get most of it but there are still some out there.
But that was really part of one’s education as well, because you’re forced to learn a lot of tunes — a lot of tunes and a lot of different styles.

It’s good ear training and it’s just good character building. It’s not all — being a musician is not necessarily about being creative all the time, it’s also about the nuts and bolts of going to work.
